content.hero_subtitle: The full-strength Tiger hash — 192 bits of security
content.p1: Tiger-192 is the original, full-strength version of the Tiger hash function by Ross Anderson and Eli Biham. It produces a 192-bit (48-character hex) hash value using all three 64-bit words of the internal state. Designed specifically for 64-bit platforms, Tiger-192 provides 96-bit collision resistance and exceptional throughput. It's one of the few hash functions that natively produces a 192-bit output.
content.what_desc: Tiger-192 processes 512-bit blocks through three passes of eight rounds each (24 rounds total). Each round uses lookup tables with 1024 entries (4 S-boxes × 256 entries × 64 bits). The algorithm maintains three 64-bit state variables (a, b, c) that are combined after all rounds to produce the 192-bit output. The key schedule multiplies message words to achieve rapid diffusion.

content.warning_desc: Tiger was designed for speed without sacrificing too much security. It achieves this through carefully chosen S-boxes and 64-bit operations. For maximum security, SHA-256 or SHA-512 are preferred. For maximum non-cryptographic speed, consider xxHash or BLAKE3.

faq.q1: Is Tiger-192 secure enough for modern use?
faq.a1: Tiger-192 provides 96-bit collision resistance. While below the 128-bit modern recommendation, no practical attacks exist. For new security applications, prefer SHA-256.
faq.a2: TTH applies Tiger-192 in a Merkle tree structure, hashing file chunks independently. This allows verifying parts of a file without downloading the whole thing. It's used in Direct Connect (DC++) P2P.
faq.a3: BLAKE3 is faster on modern hardware due to SIMD parallelism. Tiger was designed when 64-bit scalar operations were cutting-edge. For new projects prioritizing speed, BLAKE3 is the modern choice.
